subject: Cognitive Science
title: Semantic Priming
description: A micro-lesson that makes Semantic Priming usable.

hook.text: Flash the word 'bread' and people recognize 'butter' faster than 'hammer.' The first word primes the second.

buildup.text: This is semantic priming: activating one concept partially activates related concepts in the network.

discovery.text: Meyer and Schvaneveldt measured it in 1971. Related words shave 50–80 milliseconds off reaction time.

twist.text: Priming works even subliminally. A word flashed for 30 ms—too fast to see—still speeds up related words.

climax.text: This reveals that meaning isn't looked up on command. It radiates outward automatically from every word you process.

punchline.text: Every word you read lights up a neighborhood.

quiz.question: What is semantic priming?
options: One word speeding recognition of related words

details.summary: Recognizing a word is faster when preceded by a related word: doctor primes nurse. Semantic priming reveals that related concepts are linked in memory and that activating one spreads activation to neighbors. This automatic, unconscious process tells us how meaning is organized in the mind.
details.whyItMatters: Semantic priming is a cornerstone method in cognitive science. It reveals the invisible structure of meaning in the mind and how context accelerates comprehension.
takeaways: Related words speed up recognition of each other
Spreading activation connects associated concepts in memory
Priming occurs automatically and below conscious awareness

faq.question: How is semantic priming measured?
faq.answer: In a lexical decision task, participants see a prime word like bread and then must decide if a target like butter is a real word. Responses are faster for related targets than unrelated ones like butter after nurse. The speed difference, typically 20 to 50 milliseconds, measures the priming effect.

faq.question: Is semantic priming the same as free association?
faq.answer: Related but distinct. Free association measures conscious responses: what word comes to mind when you hear dog? Semantic priming measures unconscious activation: does dog speed up recognition of cat? Associative and semantic relationships overlap but can be experimentally separated.
